zh:
卷第五
隋天台智者大師說
弟子法慎記
弟子灌頂再治
釋禪波羅蜜修證第七之一
en:
Fascicle Five
Spoken by the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, of the Sui dynasty
Recorded by his disciple Fashen
Revised and edited by his disciple Guanding
Explaining Dhyāna-Pāramitā's Cultivation and Realization, Topic 7, Part 1

zh: 上已廣明內外方便，行者若能專心修習，繫念禪門，必有證驗，是故第七、廣明修證。故經言：「修我法者，證乃自知。」今明修證中，自開為四：第一、修證世間禪相；第二、修證亦世間亦出世間禪相；第三、修證出世間禪相；第四、修證非世間非出世間禪相。今第一、釋修證世間禪者，則為三：一、四禪；二、四無量心；三、四無色定。今前釋修證四禪。
en: Above, the external and internal expedient means have already been clarified at length; if the practitioner is able to apply the mind single-mindedly in cultivation, holding the dhyāna-gates in mind, realization is bound to follow — hence topic 7 now clarifies cultivation and realization at length. Hence the sūtra says: "One who cultivates my Dharma comes to know its realization for oneself."

Here, within clarifying cultivation and realization, this opens of itself into four parts: first, the marks of cultivating and realizing mundane dhyāna; second, the marks of cultivating and realizing dhyāna that is both mundane and world-transcending; third, the marks of cultivating and realizing world-transcending dhyāna; and fourth, the marks of cultivating and realizing dhyāna that is neither mundane nor world-transcending.

Here, the first is now explained: clarifying the cultivation and realization of mundane dhyāna. This itself has three parts: the four dhyānas; the four immeasurable minds; and the four formless concentrations. Here, the first is now explained: the cultivation and realization of the four dhyānas.

zh: 四禪者：一、初禪；二、二禪；三、三禪；四、四禪。今論色界根本正定，但說有四。若通方便中間，是則不定。若薩婆多人，說有未到地及中間禪，足四禪為六地定。若曇無德人，例不說有未來禪，而說有欲界定、中間禪，以為六地定。若《摩訶衍》及瞿沙所明，則具有欲界、未到地、中間禪，足四禪為七地定。此中融會，以義推之。今據正禪而論，但說有四：
en: The four dhyānas are: the first dhyāna; the second dhyāna; the third dhyāna; and the fourth dhyāna. Here, discussing the root, correct concentrations of the form realm, only four are given. If the preliminary expedient means and the intermediate dhyāna are included as well, the count is not fixed. The Sarvāstivādins hold that there is, in addition, the "not-yet-arrived" state and the intermediate dhyāna, making six stages of concentration together with the four dhyānas. The Dharmaguptakas, by contrast, do not speak of a "not-yet-arrived" state at all, but instead speak of desire-realm concentration and the intermediate dhyāna, likewise making six stages. The Mahāyāna treatise and the master Ghoṣa, however, clarify that desire-realm concentration, the "not-yet-arrived" state, and the intermediate dhyāna are all three present together, making seven stages together with the four dhyānas. These accounts may be reconciled by reasoning through their sense. Here, discussing strictly the correct dhyānas themselves, only four are given.

This opening is a methodological throat-clearing before the real work begins: different Abhidharma schools (Sarvāstivādin, Dharmaguptaka) and the Mahāyāna treatise count the preliminary stages before the "real" four dhyānas differently — six stages, or seven — purely as a matter of whether the "not-yet-arrived" state and the intermediate dhyāna between the first and second are counted as their own stages. The treatise sets this scholastic dispute aside deliberately, choosing to organize its own account strictly around the four classical dhyānas themselves, which is what the rest of this fascicle, and the most concrete, hands-on material in the entire treatise so far, is actually going to walk through in full.

zh:
第一、釋初禪修證，如經偈說：
離欲及惡法，有覺并有觀，
離生及喜樂，是人入初禪。
已得離婬火，則獲清涼定，
如人大熱悶，入冷池則樂。
如貧得寶藏，大喜覺動心。
分別則為觀，入初禪亦然。
佛此偈中具明修證初禪之相，但意難見，今當分別。就明初禪中，開為三別：第一、釋名；第二、明修習；第三、明證相。
en:
First, clarifying the cultivation and realization of the first dhyāna, as the sūtra verse says:
"Free of desire and unwholesome dharmas, possessing initial thought and sustained reflection,
Joy and happiness born of separation — such a person enters the first dhyāna.
Having already gained freedom from the fire of lust, one obtains a cool, refreshing concentration,
Like a person greatly overheated and distressed, entering a cool pool and finding joy.
Like a poor person finding a buried treasure: great joy, and initial thought stirring the mind;
Discrimination is what is called sustained reflection; entering the first dhyāna is exactly the same."
The Buddha, within this verse, clarifies in full the marks of cultivating and realizing the first dhyāna, though its intent is difficult to see at first; this shall now be distinguished. In clarifying the first dhyāna, this opens into three distinct parts: explaining the name; clarifying its cultivation; and clarifying the marks of its realization.

zh: 第一、釋名者，所言初禪者，禪名支林。行者初得支林之法，故名初禪。復次，覺觀等法，名之為支。行者修初禪覺觀之法，必於前發，故說覺觀名為初禪。問曰：若言在前發得，故為初禪者，欲界、未到地最在前發，何故不得受初禪之名？答：禪名功德叢林，欲界、未到等未有支林功德之法，雖復前發，不名初禪。復次，《摩訶衍》說欲界、未到、中間，智多而定少，是處非樂。既非正地，是故不得受初禪之名。
en: First, explaining the name: as for what is called the first dhyāna, "dhyāna" here means a grove of factors. The practitioner, first attaining this dharma of a grove of factors, is thus said to attain the first dhyāna. Furthermore, dharmas such as initial thought and sustained reflection are what is called a "factor." The practitioner's cultivation of the first dhyāna's dharma of initial thought and sustained reflection necessarily arises first, before the others — hence initial thought and sustained reflection are said to give the first dhyāna its name.

Question: if it is said that whatever arises first is thereby named "first dhyāna," then desire-realm concentration and the "not-yet-arrived" state arise earliest of all — why, then, do they not receive the name "first dhyāna"? Answer: "dhyāna" means a thicket of merit; desire-realm concentration and the "not-yet-arrived" state do not yet have the dharma of a grove of factors' merit — although they do arise first, they are not named "first dhyāna." Furthermore, the Mahāyāna treatise says that desire-realm concentration, the "not-yet-arrived" state, and the intermediate dhyāna have much wisdom but little concentration, and this state is not one of true happiness; since it is not yet the correct stage, it therefore does not receive the name "first dhyāna."

zh: 復次，言初禪者，亦名有覺有觀三昧，為有人疑言覺觀心中無定，是故佛說覺觀三昧。《地持論》說：「名覺觀俱禪。」此禪發時，必與覺觀俱發，亦名聖說法定。此定內有覺觀語言道未斷故，與說法之名，如是等種種名字不同。
en: Furthermore, what is called the first dhyāna is also named the samādhi possessing initial thought and sustained reflection — because some might doubt that concentration could be present at all within a mind of initial thought and sustained reflection, the Buddha therefore spoke of the samādhi of initial thought and sustained reflection. The Bodhisattva-bhūmi Treatise calls it "the dhyāna joined with initial thought and sustained reflection": when this dhyāna arises, it necessarily arises together with initial thought and sustained reflection. It is also called the noble concentration of expounding the Dharma, since, within this concentration, the path of language through initial thought and sustained reflection has not yet been cut off — hence it is given the name of expounding the Dharma. Such are its various differing names.

Initial thought and sustained reflection (覺 and 觀) are the very same two characters this treatise has, up to now, always translated together as "discursive thought" — the restless mental chatter that restraining-the-mind stopping is meant to restrain, and one of the fifteen unwholesome roots in fascicle 4. Here the treatise addresses that tension directly: someone might reasonably doubt that concentration could coexist with discursive thought at all, which is exactly why the first dhyāna is also named "the samādhi possessing initial thought and sustained reflection" — a name that exists specifically to reassure the doubtful. The same mental activity that scatters an untrained mind becomes, in refined form, the very thing that first admits a practitioner into dhyāna; only from the second dhyāna onward is it finally left behind entirely. From here on, this translation renders 覺 and 觀 as "initial thought" and "sustained reflection" when they appear as this pair of technical factors, to keep them distinguishable from their more general, unwholesome-root sense.

zh: 第二、明修習，復開為二：前明所修之法，後辨能修之心。第一、明所修法者，即是阿那波那，為修習根本初禪之法。就中即有三意：一、釋息名；二、辨息相；三、明用息不同。第一、所言阿那波那者，此是外國語，秦言阿那為入息，波那為出息。《安般守意三昧經》言：「安之言生，般之言滅。」若約息生滅明，義如上說；若約心生滅為語，是則不定。今用入出息為正番。
en: Second, clarifying cultivation: this, in turn, opens into two parts — first clarifying the method to be cultivated, and afterward distinguishing the mind that does the cultivating.

First, clarifying the method to be cultivated: this is precisely mindfulness of the breath, the method for cultivating the root first dhyāna. Within this, there are three parts: explaining the terms for the breath; distinguishing the marks of the breath; and clarifying the different ways the breath may be used.

First, as for what is called ānāpāna: this is a foreign term; in the Qin-dynasty translation, āna is the in-breath and apāna is the out-breath. The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Breath says: "'Ān' means arising, and 'apān' means ceasing." If explained in terms of the breath's own arising and ceasing, the sense is as given above; if spoken of in terms of the mind's arising and ceasing, this is not fixed. Here, in-breath and out-breath are taken as the correct rendering.

zh: 二、辨息相中有四：一、風；二、喘；三、氣；四、息。分別四種之相，具如調息中說。但數風則散，數喘則結，數氣則勞，數息則定。行者應當捨三存息，善取不聲不結，綿綿若存若亡之相而用之。三、明用息不同者，一師教繫心數出息。所以者何？數出息則氣不急，身不脹滿，身心輕利，易入三昧。有師教數入息，何故爾？數入息：一者、易入定，隨息內歛故；二、斷外境故；三、易見內三十六物故；四、身力輕盛故；五、內實息貪恚故。有如是等勝利非一，應數入息。有師教數入出無在，但取所便而數。無的偏用，隨人心安，入定無過，即用三師所論，皆不許出入一時俱數。何以故？以有息遮病，生在喉中，猶如草葉，吐則不出，咽則不入，此患生故。又師依四時用數，今所未詳。
en: Second, distinguishing the marks of the breath: there are four — wind; panting; breath-with-effort; and true breath. The marks of these four kinds are distinguished in full within the discussion of regulating the breath. Counting the wind leads only to scattering; counting the panting leads only to constriction; counting the breath-with-effort leads only to fatigue; counting the true breath alone leads to concentration. The practitioner should set aside the first three and retain only the true breath, skillfully taking up its mark — soundless, unconstricted, continuous, as though present and yet almost imperceptible — and using this alone.

Third, clarifying the different ways the breath may be used: one master teaches fixing the mind on counting the out-breath. Why is this? Counting the out-breath keeps the breath from becoming urgent, the body from becoming distended and full, so that body and mind grow light and agile, easily entering samādhi. Another master teaches counting the in-breath instead — why is this? Counting the in-breath: first, makes concentration easier to enter, since the breath is thereby drawn inward and gathered in; second, cuts off external objects; third, makes it easier to see the thirty-six substances within the body; fourth, makes the body's own strength light and vigorous; fifth, genuinely settles craving and anger from within. There are such benefits as these, not of one kind only, and so one should count the in-breath. Yet another master teaches that it makes no difference whether one counts the in-breath or the out-breath, and that one should simply count whichever is more convenient, with no fixed preference either way — whichever puts the practitioner's own mind at ease and allows concentration to be entered without fault is fine. But all three masters, whatever they otherwise say, agree in not permitting the in-breath and out-breath to be counted together at the same time. Why is this? Because this gives rise to the ailment of breath-obstruction, arising in the throat like a blade of grass caught there — exhaling, it will not come out, and swallowing, it will not go in; this affliction arises from counting both at once. There is also a master who teaches counting according to the four seasons, though this is not examined in detail here.

zh: 第二、明能數之心，亦為三意：一、明能數之心；二、明轉緣；三、料揀。一、明能數之心者，以細念之心攝心對息，從一至十，令心不散，故名數息。若數不滿十，名數減；若至十一，名數增。然增減之數，並非得定之道。若從一至十，恒具十，無有間一之失，故名數法成就。若於中間心竊異緣，數法則亂，是故心覺散亂義強。若以一為數者，一則無間。若有異緣，便不時覺。是以但緣一息，不能除亂。若過十者，更一法起，一心緣二，即有亂生，故名為增。夫數息者，但細心約息記數而已，不得多取數相。若息多，則氣滿腹脹體急，坐欲不安。
en: Second, clarifying the mind that does the counting: this, too, has three parts — clarifying the counting mind itself; clarifying the shift in what it takes as its object; and a concluding distinction.

First, clarifying the counting mind itself: with a fine, attentive mind, gathering the mind in and fixing it on the breath, counting from one to ten so that the mind does not scatter — this is what is called counting the breath. If the count falls short of ten, this is called a deficient count; if it reaches eleven, this is called an excessive count. Yet neither an excessive nor a deficient count is truly the path to attaining concentration. If one counts from one to ten, always completing the full ten without ever missing a single count, this is called the accomplishment of the counting method. But if, partway through, the mind secretly wanders to some other object, the counting method falls into disorder — this is precisely how one comes to recognize that the mind has scattered. If one takes "one" alone as the count for each breath, there is then no interval left open for anything else to intrude; but should some other object arise, one may fail to notice it in time. Hence, taking a single breath alone as the object is not sufficient by itself to remove disorder. If the count exceeds ten, some further factor has arisen — the mind is then taking two things as its object within a single mind, and disorder arises from just this — hence this is called an excessive count. As for counting the breath: one should simply keep count with a fine, attentive mind fixed on the breath itself, and not fuss over the mark of the counting too much. If one dwells on the breath excessively, the qi becomes overfull, the abdomen distends, and the body grows tense, so that sitting itself becomes uneasy.

zh: 二、轉緣者，初數於息，覺息微微，當置數息，便隨於息，任運出入。若心欲靜，便捨隨，凝心止住。心若闇忽，即便靜照色息。心若浮動，即便捨觀歸數及隨止也，是故名還。心不馳蕩，凝神寂慮，故名為淨。行者若能如是善巧攝錄，心則易定。第三、料揀息為初門者。問曰：一切法門悉可為初，何故但說阿那波那以為初門？答曰：不然。今依佛教，如經說：「阿那波那是三世諸佛入道初門。」是故釋迦初詣道樹，欲習佛法，內思安般，一數，二隨，乃至還、淨，具如《瑞應經》所說。
en: Second, as for the shift in what the mind takes as its object: at first, counting the breath, one becomes aware of the breath growing faint and subtle; at this point, one should set counting aside and simply follow the breath instead, letting it go out and come in of its own accord. If the mind then wishes to grow still, one should set following aside as well, fixing the mind and settling it in stillness. If the mind then grows dark and dull, one should instead calmly illuminate form and breath together. If the mind grows restless and unsettled instead, one should set contemplating aside and return to counting, following, or stilling — hence this is called returning. Once the mind no longer runs off and scatters, the spirit gathered in and every deliberation stilled, this is called purifying. If the practitioner is able to skillfully gather the mind in this way, concentration is thereby easily attained.

Third, distinguishing why the breath serves as the first gate: Question: every dharma-gate whatsoever could in principle serve as a starting point — why, then, is only mindfulness of the breath spoken of as the first gate? Answer: this does not follow. Here, in accordance with the Buddha's own teaching, the sūtra says: "Mindfulness of the breath is the first gate by which the buddhas of the three periods of time have entered the path." Hence, when Śākyamuni first arrived beneath the bodhi tree, wishing to practice the Buddhadharma, he reflected inwardly on mindfulness of the breath — first counting, second following, and on through stilling, contemplating, returning, and purifying — exactly as given in full in the Sūtra of Auspicious Manifestations.

The six-stage sequence named here in passing — counting, following, stilling, contemplating, returning, purifying — is the "six wondrous gates" (六妙門), the subject of Zhiyi's own separate, shorter treatise. Its appearance here confirms that this whole breath-counting method is the seed the six wondrous gates grow out of, worked out here in the specific service of reaching the first dhyāna rather than as its own free-standing path. The three masters' disagreement over in-breath versus out-breath versus either is characteristic of how this treatise handles real disagreements among teachers: rather than picking a winner, it reports each position's own reasoning and lets the practitioner's own ease of practice be the deciding factor — with only one point held non-negotiable, never counting both breaths at once, on pain of a genuine physical ailment.

quiz.q: Topic 7, cultivation and realization, opens into which four?
options: mundane dhyāna, both mundane and world-transcending, world-transcending, neither mundane nor world-transcending
quiz.why: "This opens of itself into four parts: first, the marks of cultivating and realizing mundane dhyāna; second ... dhyāna that is both mundane and world-transcending; third ... world-transcending dhyāna; and fourth ... dhyāna that is neither mundane nor world-transcending." The four dhyānas are only part of the first.

quiz.q: Mundane dhyāna is divided into which three?
options: the six gates, sixteen excellences, thorough-and-bright
the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless concentrations
nine contemplations, eight recollections, ten contemplations
quiz.why: "Clarifying the cultivation and realization of mundane dhyāna. This itself has three parts: the four dhyānas; the four immeasurable minds; and the four formless concentrations." The six gates belong to the second category and the nine contemplations to the third.

quiz.q: Including the preliminary and intermediate stages, how many stages of concentration do the Mahāyāna treatise and Ghoṣa count?
options: seven: desire-realm, not-yet-arrived, intermediate, plus the four dhyānas
quiz.why: "The Mahāyāna treatise and the master Ghoṣa, however, clarify that desire-realm concentration, the 'not-yet-arrived' state, and the intermediate dhyāna are all three present together, making seven stages together with the four dhyānas." The Sarvāstivādins and Dharmaguptakas each count six.

quiz.q: The Dharmaguptakas and Sarvāstivādins both count six stages. How do they differ?
options: Sarvāstivāda: not-yet-arrived and intermediate plus four; Dharmaguptaka: no not-yet-arrived, but desire-realm and intermediate plus four
quiz.why: "The Sarvāstivādins hold that there is, in addition, the 'not-yet-arrived' state and the intermediate dhyāna, making six stages ... The Dharmaguptakas, by contrast, do not speak of a 'not-yet-arrived' state at all, but instead speak of desire-realm concentration and the intermediate dhyāna, likewise making six stages."

quiz.q: What sūtra line opens topic 7, cultivation and realization?
options: dhyāna is a grove of factors
one who cultivates my Dharma comes to know its realization for oneself
quiz.why: "Above, the external and internal expedient means have already been clarified at length; if the practitioner is able to apply the mind single-mindedly in cultivation ... realization is bound to follow ... Hence the sūtra says: 'One who cultivates my Dharma comes to know its realization for oneself.'"

quiz.q: Which line belongs to the verse quoted for the first dhyāna?
options: like a poor person finding treasure, great joy stirs the mind
like emerging from a dark room
quiz.why: The first-dhyāna verse includes "Like a poor person finding a buried treasure, great joy stirs and moves the mind." The dark room belongs to the second dhyāna, the spring to the third, and still water to the second-dhyāna verse.

quiz.q: What does the text say "dhyāna" means in "first dhyāna"?
options: a grove of factors; the practitioner first attains this dharma, hence "first dhyāna"
quiz.why: "As for what is called the first dhyāna, 'dhyāna' here means a grove of factors. The practitioner, first attaining this dharma of a grove of factors, is thus said to attain the first dhyāna."

quiz.q: Desire-realm concentration and the not-yet-arrived state arise first. Why are they not called the first dhyāna?
options: they lack the merit of a grove of factors; the Mahāyāna treatise says they have more wisdom than concentration and are not the proper stage
quiz.why: "'Dhyāna' means a thicket of merit; desire-realm concentration and the 'not-yet-arrived' state do not yet have the dharma of a grove of factors' merit ... the Mahāyāna treatise says that desire-realm concentration, the 'not-yet-arrived' state, and the intermediate dhyāna have much wisdom but little concentration."

quiz.q: Which are other names for the first dhyāna?
options: the samādhi with initial thought and sustained reflection; the dhyāna joined with them; the noble concentration of expounding the Dharma
quiz.why: "What is called the first dhyāna is also named the samādhi possessing initial thought and sustained reflection ... The Bodhisattva-bhūmi Treatise calls it 'the dhyāna joined with initial thought and sustained reflection' ... It is also called the noble concentration of expounding the Dharma." Noble silence and joy belong to the second dhyāna, unmoving to the fourth.

quiz.q: Why is the first dhyāna also called the noble concentration of expounding the Dharma?
options: within it initial thought and sustained reflection remain, so the path of language is not cut off
one must hear the Dharma to enter
one can teach while in it
quiz.why: "Within this concentration, the path of language through initial thought and sustained reflection has not yet been cut off — hence it is given the name of expounding the Dharma." The second dhyāna, having extinguished them, is called noble silence.

quiz.q: How does the text explain ānāpāna?
options: āna is the in-breath, apāna the out-breath; this is the correct rendering
quiz.why: "In the Qin-dynasty translation, āna is the in-breath and apāna is the out-breath ... Here, in-breath and out-breath are taken as the correct rendering."

quiz.q: One master teaches counting the in-breath. Which benefits are listed?
options: the breath not urgent, body not distended, light and agile
easier entry into concentration, cutting off outer objects, seeing the thirty-six substances, a light vigorous body, settling craving and anger
quiz.why: "Counting the in-breath: first, makes concentration easier to enter, since the breath is thereby drawn inward and gathered in; second, cuts off external objects; third, makes it easier to see the thirty-six substances within the body; fourth, makes the body's own strength light and vigorous; fifth, genuinely settles craving and anger from within." The other list belongs to counting the out-breath.

quiz.q: Why do all three masters forbid counting the in- and out-breath together?
options: it causes breath-obstruction in the throat like a blade of grass — it will neither come out nor go down
quiz.why: "All three masters, whatever they otherwise say, agree in not permitting the in-breath and out-breath to be counted together at the same time. Why is this? Because this gives rise to the ailment of breath-obstruction, arising in the throat like a blade of grass caught there — exhaling, it will not come out, and swallowing, it will not go in."

quiz.q: In counting the breath, what are a "deficient count" and an "excessive count"?
options: falling short of ten is deficient; reaching eleven is excessive; neither leads to concentration
quiz.why: "Counting from one to ten so that the mind does not scatter — this is what is called counting the breath. If the count falls short of ten, this is called a deficient count; if it reaches eleven, this is called an excessive count. Yet neither an excessive nor a deficient count is truly the path to attaining concentration."

quiz.q: "Counting the wind leads to scattering" — what of counting the true breath, and what should the practitioner do?
options: counting true breath leads to concentration; set aside the three and keep the true breath, soundless, unconstricted, continuous
quiz.why: "Counting the wind leads only to scattering; counting the panting leads only to constriction; counting the breath-with-effort leads only to fatigue; counting the true breath alone leads to concentration. The practitioner should set aside the first three and retain only the true breath."

quiz.q: Which describes the sequence of shifting the object?
options: when the breath grows subtle, follow it; to grow still, fix the mind; if dull, illuminate; if restless, return; when no longer scattering, purify
quiz.why: "At first, counting the breath, one becomes aware of the breath growing faint and subtle; at this point, one should set counting aside and simply follow the breath instead ... If the mind then grows dark and dull, one should instead calmly illuminate form and breath together ... If the mind grows restless and unsettled instead, one should set contemplating aside and return ... this is called purifying."

quiz.q: Why is mindfulness of the breath the first gate, and what is cited?
options: "Mindfulness of the breath is the first gate by which the buddhas of the three times entered the path"; Śākyamuni at the bodhi tree reflected on it
quiz.why: "The sūtra says: 'Mindfulness of the breath is the first gate by which the buddhas of the three periods of time have entered the path.' Hence, when Śākyamuni first arrived beneath the bodhi tree ... he reflected inwardly on mindfulness of the breath."
